en: Thus have I heard— The Shorter Discourse on the Simile of the Elephant’s Footprint (Cūḷahatthipadopama-sutta), Majjhima Nikāya 27.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now on that occasion the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi was driving out from Sāvatthī in the middle of the day in a all-white chariot drawn by mares.
The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi saw the wanderer Pilotika coming in the distance.
Having seen him, he said this to the wanderer Pilotika:
"Well now, from where has Master Vacchāyana come, having traveled all day?
"Indeed, sir, I have come from the presence of the ascetic Gotama."
“What do you think, Master Vatsa, regarding the discernment of wisdom of the ascetic Gotama? Do you consider him wise?
“Who am I, sir, that I should know the discernment of wisdom of the ascetic Gotama?
Surely only someone like him would be able to know the discernment of wisdom of the ascetic Gotama.”
“Master Vacchāyana indeed praises the ascetic Gotama with lofty praise.
“Who am I, sir, that I should praise the ascetic Gotama?
That venerable Gotama is praised by those who are themselves worthy of praise; he is the supreme among gods and humans.”
“But for what reason, Master Vacchāyana, do you have such confidence in the ascetic Gotama?
“Just as if, sir, a skilled elephant woodsman were to enter an elephant wood and see in that elephant wood a large elephant’s footprint, long in extent and broad across;”
Thus he would come to the conclusion:
"Oh, what a great nāga he is!
In the same way, sir, as soon as I saw four things in the ascetic Gotama, I came to the conclusion: [he is a great nāga].
‘The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened; the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way.
What are these four?

Here, sir, I see some learned kṣatriya scholars, skillful and accomplished in the doctrines of others, like those who pierce hair with a needle; they move about as if breaking through the various speculative views with the sword of wisdom.
They hear:
"Sirs, the ascetic Gotama will indeed descend upon such-and-such a village or town.
They then formulate a question:
‘We shall approach the ascetic Gotama and ask him this question.
If he is asked thus, he will answer thus; then we shall refute his position in this way.
And if he is asked thus, he will answer thus; then we shall refute his position in that way.’
They hear:
“Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama has arrived at such-and-such a village or town.
They then approach the ascetic Gotama.
The ascetic Gotama instructs, exhorts, inspires, and gladdens them with a discourse on the Dhamma.

Having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the ascetic Gotama with a discourse on the Dhamma, they do not even question the ascetic Gotama, so how could they ever refute his doctrine?
On the contrary, they simply become disciples of the ascetic Gotama himself.
"Sir, when I saw this first point regarding the ascetic Gotama, I reached the conclusion:
'The Blessed One is a perfectly enlightened one; the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way.
Furthermore, sir, I see here certain brahmin scholars... [and so on].
Householder-scholars... [and so on] ...

ascetic-scholars who are skillful, having refuted the doctrines of others and being like hair-splitting archers—they move about, as it were, shattering those positions of views with the weapon of wisdom.
They hear:
"The ascetic Gotama, it is said, will be coming to such-and-such a village or town.
They prepare a question, thinking: "Having approached the ascetic Gotama, we shall ask him this question."
‘If he is asked in this way, he will answer in this way; then we shall refute his position.
And if he is asked in this way, he will answer in this way; then we shall likewise refute his position.
They hear: ‘The ascetic Gotama has indeed arrived at such-and-such a village or town.’”
They approach the ascetic Gotama.
The ascetic Gotama instructs, exhorts, inspires, and gladdens them with a discourse on the Dhamma.

Having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the ascetic Gotama with a discourse on the Dhamma, they do not even ask the ascetic Gotama a question, so how could they ever refute his doctrine?
On the contrary, they simply request the ascetic Gotama for permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness.
The ascetic Gotama ordains them.
Having gone forth there, dwelling secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute, before long—for the sake of which...
Noble sons go forth from the home life into homelessness for the right purpose;
having realized for themselves through direct knowledge in this very life the supreme goal of the holy life, they dwell having attained it.
They speak thus:
‘Truly, sirs, we have gained our goal; truly, sirs, we have attained our goal!
For formerly, while being non-recluses, we claimed to be recluses; while being non-Brahmins, we claimed to be Brahmins; while being non-Arahants, we claimed to be Arahants.
Now indeed we are recluses; now indeed we are Brahmins; now indeed we are Arahants.’
When I, sir, saw this fourth point in the ascetic Gotama, then I reached the conclusion:
"The Blessed One is a perfectly awakened Buddha; the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples has practiced the good way.
Since I, sir, saw these four points in the ascetic Gotama, then I reached the conclusion.
“The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened; the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way.

When this was said, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇī descended from his all-white chariot drawn by mares, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, and three times uttered this inspired exclamation:
“Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One!”
"Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One!
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One!
Perhaps we might at some time, on some occasion, meet with that Master Gotama; perhaps there might be some conversation and discussion."
Then the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side.
Sitting there, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation he had had with the wanderer Pilotika.
When this was said, the Blessed One said this to the brahmin Jāṇussoṇī:
“Brahmin, it is not by this much alone that the simile of the elephant’s footprint is fulfilled in detail.
But rather, brahmin, as to how the simile of the elephant’s footprint is fulfilled in detail:”
“Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, sir,” the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Just as if, brahmin, a forest-dweller were to enter an elephant forest.
He would see in that elephant forest a large elephant’s footprint, long in extent and broad across.
A skilled elephant-forest dweller would not yet come to the conclusion:”
‘Truly, this is a great elephant!
For what reason?
Because, brahmin, in the elephant forest there are female elephants called dwarfish ones who have large feet; this must be their footprint.
He follows it.
Following it, he sees in the elephant forest a large elephant’s footprint—long in extent, broad across, and deep where it has been trodden.
A skilled elephant-tracker does not yet reach a conclusion:
‘Great indeed, sir, is this elephant!
For what reason?
Because, brahmin, there are in the Nāga Grove female elephants called Uccā-Kālārikā who have large feet; it must be one of theirs that this is.
He follows it.
Following it, he sees in the elephant forest a large elephant’s footprint—long in extent, wide across, deep where it has been trodden, and with high marks made by the tusks.
A skilled elephant-tracker does not yet reach a conclusion:
‘Great indeed, sir, is this elephant!
For what reason?
Because, brahmin, in the elephant forest there are tall female elephants named Kaṇerukā who have large feet; this must be their footprint.
He follows it.

Following it, he sees in the elephant forest a large elephant’s footprint—long in extent, broad across, deep where it has been trodden, with high marks made by the tusks, and high marks from the breaking of branches.
And he sees that elephant, either at the foot of a tree or in the open air, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
Thus he concludes:
‘This indeed is that great nāga.

In the same way, brahmin, here a Tathāgata arises in the world—an Arahat, a perfectly enlightened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, well-gone, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.

Thus, having realized for himself through direct higher knowledge this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its recluses and brahmins, its princes and its people, he makes it known.
He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals the holy life, entirely complete and pure.
A householder, or a householder’s son, or one born into some other family hears that Dhamma.
Having heard that Dhamma, he gains faith in the Tathāgata.
Possessing that attainment of faith, he reflects thus:
"Household life is cramped, a path of dust; going forth is the open air."
"It is not easy for one living in a household to lead the holy life (brahmacariya) that is utterly perfect, utterly pure, and polished like a conch shell.
What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness?
Then, at a later time, having abandoned a small or a large mass of wealth, he went forth.

Having abandoned either a small circle of relatives or a large circle of relatives, he shaves off his hair and beard, puts on saffron-colored robes, and goes forth from the home life into homelessness.
Having thus gone forth, having entered upon the training and way of life of the bhikkhus, he abandons the taking of life; from the taking of life...
He abstains from taking life; laying aside the rod and the sword, he dwells conscientious and compassionate, sympathetic toward the welfare of all living beings.
Having abandoned taking what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given; he takes only what is given, expects only what is given, and dwells with a heart free from theft.
Having abandoned unchastity, he lives a life of chastity; he observes celibacy and abstains from the vulgar practice of sexual intercourse.
Having abandoned false speech, he abstains from false speech; he speaks the truth, is devoted to the truth, is trustworthy, reliable, and not a deceiver of the world.
Having abandoned malicious speech, he abstains from malicious speech;

having heard something here, he does not repeat it elsewhere for the purpose of dividing these people from those, nor having heard something there, does he repeat it here for the purpose of dividing those people from these. Thus, among those who are divided...

He is a reconciler of those who are divided or a provider of what is needed for those who are united; he delights in harmony, rejoices in harmony, finds joy in harmony, and speaks words that bring about harmony.

Having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech. He speaks such words as are gentle, pleasing to the ear, endearing, heart-reaching, urbane, agreeable to many people, and beloved by many people.

Having abandoned idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter; he speaks at the proper time, speaks what is true, speaks what is beneficial, speaks on the Dhamma, speaks on the Vinaya; he utters speech that is worth treasuring, timely, reasoned, measured, and connected with the goal.
He abstains from injuring seeds and plants;
he eats only one meal a day, refraining from eating at night, and abstains from eating at improper times.
He abstains from dancing, singing, instrumental music, and witnessing spectacles;
he abstains from wearing garlands, using scents and unguents, and from the practice of beautifying and adorning himself;
he abstains from high and luxurious beds and seats.
He abstains from accepting gold and silver;
he abstains from accepting raw grain;
he abstains from accepting raw meat.
He abstains from accepting women and girls;
he abstains from accepting male and female slaves;
he abstains from accepting goats and sheep.
He abstains from accepting chickens and pigs;
he abstains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses, and mares;
he abstains from accepting fields and land.
He abstains from engaging in the business of running errands and acting as a messenger;
he abstains from buying and selling;
he abstains from cheating with false scales, false weights, and false measures.
He abstains from subterfuge, deception, fraud, and crookedness;
he abstains from mutilation, execution, imprisonment, extortion, robbery, and violence.
He is content with robes that serve to protect the body and almsfood that serves to sustain the belly. Wherever he goes, he goes taking these very things with him.

Just as a winged bird, wherever it flies, flies only with its wings as its burden, even so a bhikkhu is content with robes to protect the body and almsfood to sustain the belly. Wherever he goes, he goes taking these with him.
Endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, he experiences within himself the happiness that is blameless.
Thus, having seen a form with the eye, he does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
Since, if he were to dwell with the faculty of the eye unrestrained, covetousness, dejection, and evil unwholesome states might flow in upon him, he practices for its restraint;
he guards the faculty of the eye and achieves restraint over the faculty of the eye.
Having heard a sound with the ear ... pe ...
having smelled an odor with the nose ...
having tasted a flavor with the tongue ...
Having touched a tangible object with the body...
having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one does not grasp at its signs or its secondary characteristics.
For if one dwells with this faculty of the mind unguarded, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—[might arise].
If unwholesome states were to flow into him, he practices for their restraint; he guards the faculty of the mind and attains mastery over the faculty of the mind.
Possessed of this noble restraint of the faculties, he experiences within himself the untainted happiness.
He acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; he acts with clear comprehension when looking ahead and looking aside.
He acts with clear comprehension when bending and extending his limbs; he acts with clear comprehension in carrying his outer robe, bowl, and inner robe;
he acts with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; he acts with clear comprehension in defecating and urinating;
and he acts with clear comprehension when going, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent.
Thus, endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, endowed with this noble contentment,
endowed with this noble restraint of the sense faculties, and endowed with this noble mindfulness and clear comprehension,
he resorts to a secluded lodging: a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, or a heap of straw.
Then, having returned from his almsround after the meal, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
Having abandoned covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind of covetousness.
Having abandoned ill will and hatred, he dwells with a mind free from ill will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings; he purifies his mind of ill will and hatred.
Having abandoned sloth and torpor, he dwells free from sloth and torpor, percipient of light, mindful and clearly comprehending; he purifies his mind of sloth and torpor.
Having abandoned restlessness and remorse, he dwells unagitated, with a mind inwardly calmed; he purifies his mind of restlessness and remorse.
Having abandoned doubt, he dwells as one who has crossed beyond doubt, no longer questioning regarding wholesome states; he purifies his mind of doubt.
Thus, having abandoned these five hindrances— defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—

secluded from sensual pleasures and secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first *jhāna*, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
This too, brahmin, is called a footprint of the Tathāgata, a path frequented by the Tathāgata, and a track trodden by the Tathāgata.
Yet even then, the noble disciple does not yet reach the conclusion:
"The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened; the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way.

Furthermore, brahmin, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal tranquility and singleness of mind, is without applied thought and without sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
“This too, brahmin, is said:
‘...the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing well.
Furthermore, brahmin, with the fading away of rapture, a bhikkhu dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending.”
He experiences pleasure with the body, which the Noble Ones describe as "dwelling in happiness, mindful and equanimous";
thus he enters and dwells in the third jhāna.
This too, brahmin, is called [the second fruit of the life of renunciation]... [and so on].
‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples has practiced well.
Furthermore, brahmin, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief,
a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
This too, brahmin, is called a footprint of the Tathāgata, frequented by the Tathāgata, and colored by the Tathāgata.
Yet even then, the noble disciple does not yet reach the conclusion:
"The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened; the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples has practiced the good way."

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it toward the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
He recollects his manifold past lives, that is to say: one birth, two births... [as far as] thus with their aspects and particulars he recollects his manifold past lives.
This too, brahmin, is called a footprint of the Tathāgata, a path frequented by the Tathāgata, and a track left by the Tathāgata.
Yet the noble disciple does not yet reach the conclusion:
"The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened; the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way.

With his mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs his mind to the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.
With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans... [he] understands beings as faring according to their kamma.
This too, brahmin, is called a footprint of the Tathāgata, a path frequented by the Tathāgata, and a track marked by the Tathāgata.
Yet even then, the noble disciple does not yet reach the final conclusion:
‘The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened; the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way.

With his mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs his mind toward the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.

He understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘These are the taints’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of the taints’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of the taints’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints. When he knows and sees thus, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, from the taint of existence, and from the taint of ignorance. When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being. This, monks, is called a monk who is a stream-enterer, no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination.”
One understands as it really is: "This is the cessation of suffering"; one understands as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
One understands as it really is: "These are the taints"; one understands as it really is: "This is the origin of the taints."
‘This is the cessation of the taints,’ he understands as it really is; ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of the taints,’ he understands as it really is.
This too, brahmin, is called a footprint of the Tathāgata, a path frequented by the Tathāgata, and a track marked by the Tathāgata.
But a noble disciple has not yet reached the ultimate conclusion; rather, he is reaching that conclusion:
"The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened; the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way.
For one who knows thus and sees thus, the mind is liberated from the influx of sensuality, the mind is liberated from the influx of existence, and the mind is liberated from the influx of ignorance.
When liberated, the knowledge arises: "It is liberated.
One understands: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
This too, brahmin, is called a footprint of the Tathāgata, a place frequented by the Tathāgata, and a domain delighted in by the Tathāgata.
"To this extent, brahmin, a noble disciple has reached the conclusion:
‘The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened; the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way.
To this extent, brahmin, the simile of the elephant’s footprint is fulfilled in detail."
When this was said, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi said this to the Blessed One:
“Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama!
Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost...”
Or as one might show the way to one lost in a forest, or as one might hold up an oil lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—
just so has the Dhamma been elucidated by Master Gotama in many ways.
Therefore, I go for refuge to Master Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
“May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
The Short Discourse on the Simile of the Elephant’s Footprint is finished; it is the seventh.
